title: Existentialism’s 21st‑Century Continuations - Psychology & Therapy
content_html:
Existentialism’s 21st‑Century Continuations - Psychology & Therapy

  • Mind / Process: Therapy as structured interference with memory construction and appraisal (reconsolidation, specificity, values).
  • Language / Expression: Narrative re‑authoring (life review, reminiscence) and meaning‑making as memory work.
  • Sleep / Replay / Dream: Consolidation/replay as a substrate for therapeutic change and extinction learning.
  • Substrate: Neurobiological mechanisms of memory reconsolidation that therapies may leverage.
  • Meaning / Void / Infinite: Existential positive psychology (meaning‑centered interventions) situating memory in a life‑project.

Meaning‑Centered Therapies

Logotherapy → Existential Positive Psychology

Second‑wave Positive Psychology reframes flourishing as growth through suffering and meaning‑making, explicitly building on Frankl. Practically, this centres interventions on appraisal of autobiographical memory and its integration into a coherent life project (e.g., Integrative Meaning Therapy).

Narrative Memory Work

Life Review & reminiscence

Life Review Therapy (LRT) and reminiscence use guided autobiographical retrieval and re‑evaluation to reduce depressive symptoms and strengthen identity continuity. Evidence spans RCTs and meta‑analyses, including recent updates.

Adjunctive combinations (e.g., LRT + Memory Specificity Training) target the common problem of overgeneral autobiographical memory, improving specificity and mood. [Kleijn 2018; Barry 2019]

Memory Reconsolidation

a mechanism of therapeutic change

Across modalities, a leading unifying account holds that durable therapeutic change results when maladaptive emotional memories are reactivated and updated within the reconsolidation window—integrating new, incompatible emotional learnings.

Laboratory demonstrations: brief reactivation followed by new learning can persistently attenuate conditioned fear in animals and humans when delivered within the reconsolidation boundary conditions.

EMDR and Reconsolidation‑Aligned Accounts

EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing) is hypothesized to promote adaptive reprocessing of traumatic memories; contemporary reviews discuss how EMDR effects may overlap with reconsolidation and predictive‑processing accounts.

Values‑Based Therapies (ACT) & the Self‑Memory System

Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) emphasizes values‑based action and psychological flexibility. Though not a memory therapy per se, values clarification and defusion change the interpretive frame through which autobiographical memories are encoded, retrieved, and evaluated—consistent with the Self‑Memory System (SMS) theory that links goals of the working self with autobiographical memory construction.

Memory Specificity Training (MeST)

MeST directly trains retrieval of specific autobiographical events to reduce overgeneral memory, which is implicated in depression, PTSD, and rumination. Meta‑analyses indicate improvements in both memory specificity and mood symptoms; recent clinical combinations with LRT are promising.
